name: Cape Cod Revival

revival_periods.note: Continuous production in New England and as a New Traditional and cottage-community type nationally.

lineage.note: The small, frame, one-and-a-half-storey wing of the parent style, and the only one whose proportions were seriously studied.
The claimed ancestor, and one of the few in this branch whose dimensions the revival genuinely tried to reproduce rather than inflate.
The broader New England frame vocabulary - clapboard, small sash, massive central chimney - from which the Cape is a reduction.
Convergent from about 1938: the FHA-standard minimal house and the Cape Cod Revival cottage become nearly the same building, and the reciprocal claim is recorded on both nodes.

description.short: The small, steep-roofed, one-and-a-half-storey frame house that Royal Barry Wills and the FHA between them made the default American starter home from 1935 to 1960, and the one revival in this branch that shrank its model rather than inflating it.
description.long:
Cape Cod Revival is unusual in this family for treating its historical model as a discipline rather than as a costume. The eighteenth-century Cape is a very tightly reasoned building: a rectangular box a room and a half deep, one and a half storeys, a massive central chimney, a steep gable roof to shed snow, an eave line dropped almost onto the window heads to reduce wind exposure, and no ornament except a door surround. The revival keeps almost all of that. What it adds is a dormer or two, a cellar, plumbing, and a garage; what it changes is that the chimney stops being structural and starts being an emblem.

Royal Barry Wills is the reason it is a style rather than a survival. Working from a Boston office from 1925, Wills spent thirty years measuring, publishing, and refining the type, and he was explicit that the whole thing lived or died on proportion. His office standards are worth repeating because they are exactly the sort of enforceable number this taxonomy exists to record: roof pitch between 8:12 and 10:12; eaves set just above the second-floor window heads; sash with 24 to 36 lights; clapboards graduated from about 2 3/4 in. exposure at the water table to 4 1/4 in. near the eave, so that the wall appears to rise. In 1938 Life magazine paired four modern and four traditional architects against each other for real client families; in the $5,000-$6,000 bracket Wills was set against Frank Lloyd Wright, and the family chose Wills. That result is the clearest single piece of evidence about mid-century American taste that exists.

The economics finished what the design started. The FHA's mortgage-insurance underwriting after 1934 favoured exactly this footprint - small, detached, expandable, on a modest lot - and after 1945 the veterans' housing programmes and the merchant builders adopted it wholesale. Levitt & Sons built roughly seventeen thousand houses at Levittown, New York, between 1947 and 1951, and the first model was a Cape. That is the moment the American production home acquires its default vocabulary, and it is a Colonial Revival vocabulary.

A Cape Cod house is small in a way that reads as deliberate rather than as poor, and the reason is the eave. Because the eave line sits within a foot or so of the upper window heads, the wall is very short and the roof is very large, and the building crouches. There is no shadow line to speak of, no cornice, no projection; the whole thing is one taut skin with a door in the middle of it and a chimney coming out of the ridge. Inside, the ground floor is compact and low and the upper floor is all sloped ceiling and dormer, and the effect - the reason people keep buying them - is that a very small building feels finished rather than incomplete.

defining_characteristics: One-and-a-half storeys, rectangular in plan, with a steeply pitched side-gable roof
Eave line carried low, within roughly 12 in. of the second-floor window heads, producing a short wall and a dominant roof
Central chimney on the ridge, or paired end chimneys, expressed as mass
Symmetrical three- or five-bay front with a centred entrance and a modest pilastered or hooded door surround
Multi-light double-hung sash, 6/6 or 8/12, small in individual dimension relative to the wall
Minimal ornament: no cornice beyond a simple moulding, no corner boards beyond a plain board, no porch beyond a stoop
diagnostic_tells: Second-floor windows sit in dormers or in the gable ends, never in a full-height side wall. A full second storey makes it a Colonial Revival, not a Cape.
Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12 with the eave nearly touching the upper window heads; a 6:12 roof with a tall wall is Minimal Traditional.
The chimney is on the ridge at or near the centre. A gable-end chimney is acceptable in pairs; an off-centre single stack is a builder's compromise.
No cornice, no returns, no frieze board. The presence of a modillioned cornice means the house has left this variant.

Against the eighteenth-century original: revival Capes have dormers (the originals rarely did), a full cellar, larger sash, and a chimney that no longer contains the cooking hearth and the structural core.

distinguished_from.difference: The original, c. 1690-1850, is a shingled or clapboarded box with a genuinely structural central chimney stack 6-8 ft square containing multiple hearths, almost never dormered, with tiny sash and no cellar stair to speak of. The revival keeps the silhouette and the proportional discipline but hollows out the chimney and cuts dormers into the roof.
This is the parent style at one and a half storeys with the ornament removed. A Cape that grows a full second floor, a cornice, and a portico has become general Colonial Revival.

Minimal Traditional, the FHA type of 1935-1950, has a low roof pitch of 4:12 to 6:12, a shallow eave, a tall wall, and no chimney of consequence. It is what a Cape becomes when the builder economises on roof framing.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof pitch against wall height. The type is generated by pulling the eave down to the upper window heads, which fixes the wall height, which fixes everything else. Wills's office treated graduated clapboard exposure as a second proportional device operating on the wall itself.
typical_ratios: Wall height from grade to eave 11-13 ft for the full one-and-a-half storeys
Eave soffit within 12 in. of the second-floor window heads
Overall footprint 24-28 ft deep by 32-40 ft wide - a plan proportion near 1:1.4
Sash of 24-36 lights total per window; graduated clapboard exposure from 2 3/4 in. at the water table to 4 1/4 in. near the eave
Door surround overall width not exceeding 5'6" for a 2'8"-3'0" leaf
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three bays on the half Cape and three-quarter Cape, five bays on the full Cape, at 7'6"-9'0" on centre. The rhythm is tighter than general Colonial Revival because the original framing bay is genuinely being reproduced.

massing_affinities.note: The variant is this massing; the half, three-quarter and full Cape are its three states.
The rear lean-to extension, which Wills used constantly to add a kitchen or family room without breaking the front.
Where the Cape grows to a full two storeys it stops being this variant and becomes plain Colonial Revival.
A gambrel over a Cape footprint is a Dutch Colonial Revival move, not a Cape one.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12, and the eave soffit must sit not more than 12 in. above the second-floor window head line. A tall wall with a low roof is Minimal Traditional and is not this variant.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. The eave-soffit-to-second-floor-window-head offset (not more than 12in, matching window_head_to_cornice_offset_in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Maximum two full storeys of wall is forbidden: the front wall may not exceed 13'0" from grade to eave. All upper-floor light on the front and rear must come from dormers.

test.note: Tests the front-wall grade-to-eave cap. 'All upper-floor light on the front and rear must come from dormers' has no matching vocabulary variable for light source and stays prose.

constraints.statement: A masonry chimney is required, on the ridge at or near the centre or paired at the gable ends, minimum 3'0" x 3'0" in plan for a central stack and rising not less than 2'0" above the ridge.

test.note: Tests the ridge-rise minimum. Chimney position (ridge-centre vs. paired gable-end, expressible via chimney_position but not tested here) and the 3'0"x3'0" plan footprint (no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Dormers, where used, must total not more than 50 percent of the roof length on any one slope, with their faces set back not less than 12 in. from the wall plane and their ridges not less than 18 in. below the main ridge.

Ornament is limited to the door surround, a simple 4-6 in. eave moulding, and 4-6 in. corner boards. Cornice returns, modillions, friezes, pediments over windows, and full-width porches are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the eave moulding width. The door surround (undimensioned), the corner-board width (also 4-6in but a distinct element with no vocabulary variable of its own), and the forbidden-ornament list stay prose.

exemplars.name: Royal Barry Wills House
exemplars.note: The architect's own house and the reference example for his office's Cape standards; later extended to the rear.

exemplars.name: Life magazine 'Eight Houses for Modern Living' Wills house
exemplars.note: Royal Barry Wills. The traditional entry chosen by the client family over Frank Lloyd Wright's modern design in the same income bracket.

exemplars.name: Levittown Cape Cod model
exemplars.note: Levitt & Sons. The first mass-produced model at Levittown, 1947-49, and the vehicle by which the type became the American postwar default.

exemplars.name: Webber House
exemplars.note: Harry Morton Ramsay. Included as a contemporaneous Boston-area point of comparison; see garrison-revival, where its overhang places it.

sources: Royal Barry Wills, Houses for Good Living (1940)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Richard Wills and Kevin Bone, At Home in New England: Royal Barry Wills Architects 1925 to Present (2013)
Barbara Kelly, Expanding the American Dream: Building and Rebuilding Levittown (1993)

proportion_packs.note: Governs the composed front as a whole: the odd bay count (three or five), the pier arithmetic, and the ranking of horizontals. Cape Cod Revival is the one node in this branch whose facade is nearly pure void-in-wall with almost no cornice to speak of, so this pack's bay-count and solid-to-void rules do the work that a heavier order would do elsewhere in the family; the pack's own three-horizontal ranking is deliberately not fully used here, since the style forbids a projecting cornice and works mostly off the water table and the head datum.

The rectangle of the door and window openings and, in particular, the single-head-datum rule, which is exactly what Wills's office standard is describing when it fixes the eave 'just above the second-floor window heads' -- there is only one head line on the front and the whole silhouette depends on it staying level and low.

Explicitly applicable and load-bearing here: the node's own hard constraints and typical ratios specify 6/6 or 8/12 sash with 24-36 lights total, and Wills's graduated clapboard exposure (2 3/4 in at the water table rising to 4 1/4 in near the eave) is exactly the kind of measured, dated device this pack exists to record.

The node's own bay_rhythm is explicit that 'the rhythm is tighter than general Colonial Revival because the original framing bay is genuinely being reproduced' (7'6"-9'0" bay, matching the pack's 16-20 ft frame-bay logic scaled to a one-and-a-half storey house). The pack's own closing note names Cape Cod Revival directly as the test case for this discipline: a correct-looking exterior wrapped around a plan no frame would produce is exactly the failure this pack is written to catch.

Interior trim only, and reduced in scale from the parent style's: a Cape's baseboard, chair rail and door casing are classical-family (raised panel doors, simple backband) rather than craftsman flat stock, but run thin and plain to suit an 11-13 ft ground-floor room rather than a high-style Georgian one. Exterior ornament is explicitly capped by the node's own hard constraint c05 -- door surround, a 4-6 in eave moulding, and corner boards only, with cornice returns, modillions and porches forbidden -- so this pack's exterior wall-section family (water table, belt, entablature) is not invoked; only the interior assemblies are.

Judgment binding: cape-cod-revival is not in this pack's own applies_to list, but the node's lineage names cape-cod-colonial -- which IS in that list -- as the ancestor whose dimensions 'the revival genuinely tried to reproduce rather than inflate,' and the whole point of the style, per its own description, is discipline rather than costume. The pack's daylight-limited, span-and-hearth-constrained 'ordinary room' logic fits a Cape's low storey (11-13 ft to the eave) far better than room-harmonic's Palladian saloons, which this variant's own text never invokes.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes present the Gibbs Doric as a full order whose four real divergences from Vignola are the Attic base, modillions replacing mutules, the cornice restated in five equal blocks, and twenty-four flutes -- three of the four being facts about a modillioned cornice on a fluted column. The node's diagnostic tell states that a modillioned cornice means the house has left this variant, which is a definitional refusal of the pack's own headline feature rather than a general disclaimer about proportional systems. The pack dimensions cornice, pediment, modillion_dentil and crown, and the node's c05 forbids modillions, friezes and pediments while the resolved kit binds frieze and cornice_return forbidden.
declined_packs.quote: No cornice, no returns, no frieze board. The presence of a modillioned cornice means the house has left this variant.
declined_packs.note: Measured --impact: governs 0 slots; declining changes no dimension on this node and no slot loses all dimensioning. Of the 7 slots the pack dimensions, ceiling_height_rule is currently governed by log-module (via swiss-chalet), chair_rail by storey-graduation (via colonial-revival), modillion_dentil by greek-doric (via greek-classical), window_head_masonry by opening-pointed (via gothic-revival-british); cornice, crown and pediment are governed by no pack on this node either way. --pair reports no live gate: endorsing would change no behaviour, only the meter.
